[EMERGING] Space plasma can calm its own waves without particles colliding, and AI just learned the trick.

The effect, called Landau damping, is something simple fluid models of plasma leave out. A team from Queen Mary University of London, the University of Colorado Boulder and Italy's CNR trained a Fourier neural operator inside a fluid solver. A single trained model reproduced both weak and strong damping and stayed numerically stable in independent simulations.

Reality check: this is one-dimensional electrostatic plasma, and the team calls it a modeling demonstration, not a new space-weather forecasting system. No speedup figures were reported.

Sources (link in bio):
Journal of Plasma Physics, 30 Oct 2026, doi.org/10.1017/S0022377826102517
Queen Mary University of London news, 1 Nov 2026

[TODAY] Every computer is secretly a heater that does math on the side.

Chips turn electricity into calculations, and that power ends up as heat that has to be carried away. In AI data centers, the International Energy Agency says one server rack can produce heat equal to 30 natural gas boilers.

The IEA projects global data center electricity use roughly doubling, from 485 TWh in 2025 to 950 TWh by 2030, about 3% of world demand. Caveat: these are projections, and the IEA also notes energy use per AI task has been falling by at least an order of magnitude a year recently.

Sources (link in bio):
IEA, Key Questions on Energy and AI, executive summary, iea.org

[IMAGINE] What if every new AI data center had to keep a town warm? 🔥

It is not pure fantasy. Al Jazeera reports that a supercomputer at the University of Southern Denmark in Sonderborg sends its waste heat into a district heating network, and Stockholm has fed data center heat into its network since 2014.

The speculative part is making it the rule. Heat loses value over distance, so it only helps where homes, schools or pools sit nearby, and today's examples are mostly Scandinavian. Several claims in the coverage come from a company that sells the cooling hardware.

Where would you build the next one? Tell us in the comments.

4:
[EMERGING] Could quantum hardware come off the same production lines as ordinary chips?

Researchers at CIC nanoGUNE in Spain, with Quantum Motion, the London Centre for Nanotechnology, Imperial College London and the University of Cambridge, built a superinductor inside a silicon chip made with a commercial CMOS process. It uses titanium nitride and serves as a key part of an ultra-sensitive charge sensor. The work is published in Nature Electronics.

Reality check: this is a sensor component, not a qubit. The preprint reports tests on only a few devices at 350 millikelvin, and fast spin-qubit readout is the team's next goal, not a result.

Sources (link in bio):
CIC nanoGUNE news, 4 Nov 2026
arXiv 2507.13202 (preprint)

5:
[EMERGING] Change the locks before anyone owns the master key. That is post-quantum cryptography in one line.

Much of today's encryption depends on math problems that a large future quantum computer could shortcut. In 2024, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology published FIPS 203, a standard called ML-KEM, whose security rests on a lattice problem known as Module Learning with Errors. It comes in three security levels.

Reality check: NIST's own wording is that ML-KEM is believed to be secure, even against attackers with a quantum computer. That is strong expert confidence, not a mathematical proof.

Sources (link in bio):
NIST, FIPS 203, 13 Aug 2024, csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/203/final

[IMAGINE] What if a quantum computer's best teammate turns out to be a supercomputer fixing its errors on the fly?

IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge National Laboratory announced a platform that pairs IBM's 120-qubit Nighthawk processor with Oak Ridge's Umbra supercomputer, which runs on AMD GPUs, to test new error-correction codes and decoders. The Department of Energy target is 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028.

Reality check: this comes from a company press release, and the 2028 figures are goals, not results. The speculative part is a future where quantum and classical machines work as one system.

[TODAY] In 2017, just 2% of new US utility-scale solar capacity had a battery beside it. This year, it is over 16%.

That is the U.S. Energy Information Administration's count as of September 2026. Developers' reported plans for the last months of the year suggest the share could reach 19%, and plans for 2027 and 2028 point above 30%. California, Arizona, New Mexico and Nevada already run at more than double the national share.

Reality check: the forward-looking figures are plans, not operating plants, and solar and battery halves of a project often start up at different times.

[TODAY] A car that can hit 120 mph doesn't average 120 mph. Power plants are the same.

Capacity factor compares the electricity a plant actually generated with what it could have produced running at full power all year. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, US nuclear plants ran at 91.1% in 2025, geothermal at 65.9%, hydro at 34.4% and wind at 33.8%.

Reality check: a lower number is not a failure. Wind and hydro depend on weather and water, and a grid mixes sources with different strengths. Capacity factor tells you how often, not how useful.

Sources (link in bio):
U.S. EIA, Electric Power Annual, Table 4.08.B

9:
[IMAGINE] What if AI data centers became the grid's shock absorbers, slowing training runs when power runs short?

The trend behind the question is real. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2025 update on US data center energy use projects data centers could account for 11.8% of US electricity by 2030 in its reference case, within a range of 9.5% to 15.3%.

The speculative part: some AI work, like training, may not need to run at a fixed hour. If it could pause during peaks and catch up when power is plentiful, a big new load could also become a flexible one. Whether that fits real schedules and contracts is an open question.

What would it take for that to work? Tell us in the comments.

Sources (link in bio):
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, United States Data Center Energy Usage Report: 2025 Update, June 2026
